story: Ines rents a bedroom in a house in Hamilton owned by Gerald, who lives there too. She shares Gerald's kitchen and the only full bathroom. In the same house, Marco rents the basement, which has its own kitchen, its own bathroom and a separate locking entrance. Both signed Gerald's one-page lease, which says: 'The Residential Tenancies Act does not apply to this agreement.' Gerald has a cat that Ines is allergic to. Last night Gerald told both of them, by text, to be out by the end of the week.
question: Does the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 apply to Ines, to Marco, or to both? What effect does the clause in the lease have?
modelAnswer: It turns on who shares a kitchen or bathroom with the owner. The Act does not apply to living accommodation whose occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner (or the owner's spouse, child or parent, or the spouse's child or parent), where that person lives in the building (s. 5 (i)). Ines shares Gerald's kitchen and bathroom and Gerald lives in the house, so her room falls within that exemption and the Act, including the Landlord and Tenant Board process, does not cover her arrangement. Marco does not share a kitchen or bathroom with Gerald, so the s. 5 (i) exemption does not reach him on these facts. The lease clause cannot take Marco outside the Act: the Act applies to rental units 'despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary' (s. 3 (1)), and a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void (s. 4 (1)). For Marco, a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act (s. 37 (1)), so a text telling him to leave by the end of the week does not by itself end his tenancy. The cat is not relevant to which law applies.

story: Dev is renting a one-bedroom apartment in Ottawa for $2,000 a month starting December 1. Before he signs, the landlord, Rosalind, asks for first month's rent, last month's rent, and a $1,000 'damage deposit' that she says she will hold until he moves out and keep back for any repairs. Dev owns a large dog, which the lease allows.
question: How much of the $1,000 damage deposit is Rosalind allowed to keep at the end of the tenancy, and for what kinds of damage?
modelAnswer: The question assumes a residential landlord may take a damage deposit. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 she may not. 'The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106' (s. 105 (1)). A 'security deposit' includes money held as security for the performance of the tenant's obligations or to be returned on a condition (s. 105 (2)), which describes a damage deposit. A rent deposit is lawful if the landlord requires it on or before entering into the tenancy agreement (s. 106 (1)), and it may not be more than the lesser of one rent period's rent and one month's rent (s. 106 (2)), here $2,000. The landlord must apply it to the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy ends (s. 106 (10)) and must pay interest on it annually at the guideline rate (s. 106 (6)). If Dev pays the $1,000, he may apply to the Board for an order that it be paid back as money collected in contravention of the Act (s. 135 (1)), within one year after it was collected (s. 135 (4)). Separately, a tenant is responsible for repairing undue damage caused by wilful or negligent conduct (s. 34); that duty exists without any deposit.

story: Fatima moved into a Kingston apartment in May 2023 at $1,600 a month and paid a $1,600 last month's rent deposit. Her rent has since been lawfully increased and is now $1,690. Her landlord, a small family company, has never paid her any interest on the deposit. He has now written to ask for $90 'to top up the deposit'. He also complains that Fatima keeps her bicycle on the balcony.
question: Can the landlord require the $90 top-up, and what can Fatima do about the interest she was never paid?
modelAnswer: Yes, a top-up is allowed: if the lawful rent increases after a rent deposit has been paid, the landlord may require the tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the deposit up to the amount permitted (s. 106 (3)), which is the lesser of one rent period's rent and one month's rent (s. 106 (2)), here $1,690. On interest, the landlord 'shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline' in effect when the payment becomes due (s. 106 (6)). The landlord may deduct from the interest owed the amount by which the maximum permitted deposit exceeds the deposit paid, and the deducted amount is treated as part of the deposit (s. 106 (7)), so the shortfall can be met out of interest owed. Where the landlord has failed to pay interest when due, the tenant may deduct the amount of that payment from a later rent payment (s. 106 (9)). The bicycle has nothing to do with the deposit.

story: Liam is moving into a Toronto apartment with rent of $1,950 a month. The building's property manager tells him that before he gets the keys he must pay last month's rent of $1,950, a $300 non-refundable 'key and fob fee', and a $150 'application processing fee'. Liam pays all of it on August 15, 2026 so he will not lose the unit. A friend tells him the property manager is not the owner, so the rules for landlords do not apply to him.
question: Were these payments lawful, is the friend right, and how and within what time can Liam try to get money back?
modelAnswer: The last month's rent is a permitted rent deposit, because it does not exceed one month's rent (ss. 105 (1), 106 (2)). The other two charges run into s. 134: unless the regulations prescribe otherwise, no landlord shall collect or require from a tenant or prospective tenant 'a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable' (s. 134 (1) (a)). A non-refundable key and fob fee and an application processing fee are amounts of that kind; whether a regulation creates an exception for a particular charge would have to be checked in the regulations themselves. The friend is wrong: the same prohibition applies to a 'superintendent, property manager or other person who acts on behalf of a landlord', with or without the landlord's authority (s. 134 (2)). Liam may apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent pay back money collected in contravention of the Act (s. 135 (1)); a prospective tenant can also apply (s. 135 (2)). No order is made on an application filed more than one year after the money was collected (s. 135 (4)), so the year runs from August 15, 2026.

story: Kwame has rented an apartment in Sudbury since March 1, 2025 at $1,500 a month. His rent has never been increased. On December 15, 2025 his landlord slipped a handwritten note under his door: 'Rent goes to $1,600 starting February 1, 2026.' The building has been rented to tenants since the 1970s. The note also says the hallway carpet will be replaced in the spring.
question: How much notice must a landlord give before raising the rent, how often can rent go up, and does this note meet those rules?
modelAnswer: Three rules apply. Notice: a landlord shall not increase the rent 'without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice' (s. 116 (1)), and the notice must be in a form approved by the Board and set out the new rent (s. 116 (3)). A handwritten note given December 15 for an increase on February 1 gives fewer than 90 days and is not the Board's form. An increase 'is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice' (s. 116 (4)). Frequency: rent may be increased only if at least 12 months have elapsed since the last increase or, if there has been none, since the unit was first rented to that tenant (s. 119 (1)); February 1, 2026 is less than 12 months after March 1, 2025. Amount: during a tenancy the increase cannot exceed the guideline except under s. 126 or 127 or an agreement under s. 121 or 123 (s. 120 (1)), and the guideline for any year is not more than 2.5 per cent (s. 120 (2)). A $100 increase on $1,500 is about 6.7 per cent, above that cap, so it would need one of those listed exceptions. The carpet replacement does not change any of this.

story: In 2024 Sophie signed a lease for a unit in a new condominium tower in Mississauga. The tower was completed and first lived in during 2022, and her landlord owns just that one unit. Sophie has now received a notice of rent increase on the Board's form, given more than 90 days ahead, raising her rent by 9 per cent, effective 13 months after she moved in. Her neighbour in an older building got only a 2.5 per cent increase this year.
question: Since the provincial rent increase guideline caps every residential rent increase in Ontario at 2.5 per cent, Sophie can refuse to pay anything above the guideline, right?
modelAnswer: No, the guideline does not cover every unit. Under s. 6.1 (2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, sections 120 (the guideline), 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132, 133, 165 and 167 do not apply to a rental unit in a building where no part of the building 'was occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018'. A tower first lived in during 2022 fits that description, and Sophie's tenancy agreement was made in 2024, after November 15, 2018, so the carve-back in s. 6.1 (4) for older tenancy agreements does not apply. The guideline cap therefore does not limit her increase. The rules that s. 6.1 (2) does not list still apply: the landlord must give at least 90 days written notice (s. 116 (1)), and at least 12 months must have passed since the unit was first rented to her or since her last increase (s. 119 (1)). On the facts given, both are met. If the exemption is disputed at the Board, 'the onus is on the landlord to prove that the subsection applies' (s. 6.1 (6)).

story: Helene personally owns a semi-detached house in London, Ontario, and rents the whole house month to month to Raj for $2,200, due on the first of each month. In early October 2026 she tells Raj that her adult son is moving back from Vancouver and will live in the house for at least two years, and that she will serve the proper Board notice. Raj works night shifts and says he would rather leave early if he finds a place before her date.
question: What is the minimum notice period for Helene's notice and what date must it end on, does Raj receive compensation, and can Raj leave before her termination date?
modelAnswer: A landlord may end a tenancy if she in good faith requires possession for residential occupation for at least one year by, among others, a child of the landlord (s. 48 (1) (c)), but only where the unit is owned at least in part by an individual and the landlord is an individual (s. 48 (5)), which Helene is. The notice must be in the Board's form (s. 43 (1)). Notice period: the termination date 'shall be at least 60 days after the notice is given and shall be the day a period of the tenancy ends' (s. 48 (2)); for this monthly tenancy that means the end of a rental month. Compensation: the landlord must pay one month's rent ($2,200) or offer another rental unit acceptable to the tenant (s. 48.1 (1)). That does not apply if the notice is given on or after the day the 2025 amendment came into force (21/09/2026 in the saved text's amendment table), sets a termination date at least 120 days after the notice is given, and that date is the end of a tenancy period (s. 48.1 (2)). So with 60 to 119 days' notice, one month's rent is owed; with at least 120 days, ending at the end of a period, none is. Leaving early: a tenant who receives this notice may end the tenancy earlier than the landlord's date (s. 48 (3)) by giving at least 10 days' notice (s. 48 (4)). If Helene applies to the Board to evict, she must file an affidavit sworn by the person who personally requires the unit (s. 72 (1) (a)).

story: Bayview Holdings Inc. owns a fourplex in Barrie and is the landlord on every lease. Its sole director and shareholder, Antonio, wants his daughter to move into Unit 3, which Grace rents. Grace has received a notice ending her tenancy because the 'landlord requires the unit for a family member', signed by Antonio on behalf of Bayview Holdings Inc. and giving her 120 days. Grace recently complained about a leaking ceiling.
question: Because the notice gives more than the minimum time and Antonio's daughter really will move in, Grace has no choice but to move out by the date in the notice. Correct?
modelAnswer: Two parts of that are wrong. First, the own-use termination in s. 48 is not available to every landlord: the section 'does not authorize a landlord to give a notice of termination of a tenancy with respect to a rental unit unless' the unit is owned in whole or in part by an individual and the landlord is an individual (s. 48 (5)). Here the owner and landlord is a corporation, so s. 48 does not authorize this notice, however long the notice period and whoever will move in. Second, a notice does not on its own force a tenant out. A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act (s. 37 (1)), and a landlord shall not recover possession unless the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit or a Board eviction order has authorized it (s. 39). Even for a valid own-use notice, the Board cannot make an eviction order without an affidavit from the person who personally requires the unit (s. 72 (1) (a)). The leaking ceiling is a separate matter under the landlord's duty to keep the unit in a good state of repair (s. 20 (1)).

story: Paulette moved out of her Windsor apartment on March 31, 2026 after her landlord, Victor, served her a notice saying his mother needed the unit to live in. In late July 2026 Paulette saw the same apartment advertised for rent online at $600 a month more than she had paid. Her new apartment costs her $450 a month more, and she paid $1,100 for movers. She has heard that Victor's mother still lives in Leamington.
question: If I take Victor to the Landlord and Tenant Board, will I win? How strong is my case?
modelAnswer: CourtSimplified does not judge whether a case will succeed or how strong it is; that is for the Board to decide after hearing both sides. What it can do is set out what the Act requires and what Paulette needs to put together. On a former tenant's application, the Board may make orders if the landlord gave a notice under s. 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated as a result of the notice, and none of the persons named in s. 48 (1) (here, the landlord's parent) occupied the unit within a reasonable time after she left (s. 57 (1) (a)). It is presumed, 'unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities', that the notice was given in bad faith if, in the period from the notice until one year after the tenant vacates, the landlord 'advertises the rental unit for rent' (s. 57 (5) (a), (6)). The application must be made no more than one year after she vacated the unit (s. 57 (2)). The orders available include payment of increased rent for one year after vacating, general compensation of up to 12 months of her last rent, reasonable moving and storage expenses, and an administrative fine (s. 57 (3)). Next steps: keep a dated copy of the listing, the notice she received, her new lease, and the movers' receipt, and file within the one-year period.

story: Noor rents an apartment in Brampton for $2,100, due on the first of each month. She lost shifts at work and did not pay the rent due November 1, 2026. On November 5, 2026 her landlord handed her a notice of termination for non-payment of rent. The same week her car broke down. Noor also has an unresolved complaint about a broken dishwasher.
question: How soon after the notice can the termination date be, how can Noor stop the termination, and is the landlord under any deadline to apply to the Board?
modelAnswer: Where a tenant fails to pay rent lawfully owing, the landlord may give notice of termination 'effective not earlier than the 7th day after the notice is given' (s. 59 (1), as amended by the Fighting Delays, Building Faster Act, 2025). The notice must set out the rent due and say that the tenant can avoid termination by paying, on or before the termination date, the rent due plus any additional rent that has come due by the date of payment (s. 59 (2)). The notice is void if, before the day the landlord applies to the Board, the tenant pays the arrears and the additional rent that would have been due (s. 59 (3)). The landlord may not apply before the day after the termination date in the notice (s. 74 (1)), and even after an application is filed, it shall be discontinued if, before the eviction order issues, the Board is satisfied that she has paid the arrears, the additional rent that would have been due, and the landlord's application fee (s. 74 (2)). As for the landlord's timing: the usual rule that an application may not be made later than 30 days after the termination date does not apply to an application based on non-payment of rent (s. 69 (2), (3)), and a non-payment notice is not one that becomes void 30 days after its termination date (s. 46 (2)). If the case goes to a hearing and Noor wants to raise her own issue, such as the dishwasher, she must give the landlord advance written notice within the time in the Rules and, unless the regulations provide otherwise, pay half of the rent arrears claimed before the hearing (s. 82 (1), (2)).

story: Before signing his lease in Thunder Bay, Mateo noticed a cracked bedroom window and black mould around the bathtub. The landlord said, 'That's how it is, take it or leave it,' and Mateo signed. Six months later winter has arrived, snow blows in through the window, and the mould has spread to the ceiling. Mateo pays his rent on time and has emailed the landlord twice about both problems. He also wishes the unit had a dishwasher.
question: Since Mateo saw the cracked window and the mould before he signed, he accepted the unit as it was and cannot make the landlord fix them, can he?
modelAnswer: That is not the law. A landlord is responsible for 'providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards' (s. 20 (1)), and that duty applies even if the tenant knew of the non-repair 'or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement' (s. 20 (2)). A clause or condition saying otherwise would be void as inconsistent with the Act (s. 4 (1)). Mateo may apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for an order determining that the landlord has breached s. 20 (1) (s. 29 (1), para. 1), within one year after the conduct occurred (s. 29 (2)). If the Board finds a breach, it may, among other things, order an abatement of rent, authorize a repair and order the landlord to pay its cost, order the landlord to do specified repairs within a set time, or order payment of his reasonable out-of-pocket expenses (s. 30 (1)). In choosing the remedy the Board must consider whether the tenant told the landlord about the problems before applying (s. 30 (2)), so his two emails are worth keeping. The missing dishwasher is not a repair issue.

story: Chloe rents a condominium unit in Waterloo from its owner, Benoit. Her lease says: 'Landlord may enter at any time for inspection.' On a Tuesday at 9 p.m. Benoit texts her: 'Coming tomorrow at 7 a.m. with a painter to look at the walls.' Last month, while Chloe was at work, Benoit let himself in to show the unit to someone thinking of buying it, without telling her. Chloe has not given notice to leave and there was no emergency. Chloe also owes the condominium $40 for a replacement parking fob.
question: Were Benoit's entries lawful, what is the effect of the lease clause, and what can Chloe do?
modelAnswer: A landlord may enter only in accordance with s. 26 or 27 (s. 25). Without written notice, entry is allowed in an emergency or if the tenant consents at the time of entry (s. 26 (1)); entry without notice to show the unit is allowed only to prospective tenants, and only where the tenancy is ending by agreement or notice (s. 26 (3)). Neither applies to either visit. To do work in the unit, the landlord needs written notice given 'at least 24 hours before the time of entry' (s. 27 (1), para. 1), specifying the reason, the day, and a time 'between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.' (s. 27 (3)). A message at 9 p.m. for 7 a.m. the next day gives less than 24 hours and names a time outside those hours. Showing the unit to a potential purchaser also requires at least 24 hours' written notice (s. 27 (2)), which was not given. The lease clause allowing entry 'at any time' is inconsistent with the Act and void (s. 4 (1)). Chloe may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord illegally entered the unit (s. 29 (1), para. 6), within one year after the entry (s. 29 (2)). If the Board so finds, it may order the landlord not to do it again, order an abatement of rent, order payment of out-of-pocket expenses, impose an administrative fine, or make any other appropriate order (s. 31 (1)). The parking fob charge is unrelated.

story: Tyrone is two months behind on rent for his Oshawa apartment. He has never received a notice of termination and there has been no Landlord and Tenant Board hearing. On Friday he came home to find the lock changed, a sign on the door reading 'Evicted for non-payment', and his furniture stacked in the building's garage. The superintendent told him the landlord will throw everything out on Monday unless he pays the arrears in full. Tyrone is staying with his sister, and the apartment is still empty.
question: What legal issues does this raise, and what can Tyrone ask the Board to do?
modelAnswer: Possession: a landlord 'shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless' the tenant has vacated or abandoned it or a Board eviction order has authorized it (s. 39). Tyrone did neither and there is no order; a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act (s. 37 (1)). Locks: a landlord shall not alter the locking system during the tenant's occupancy without giving replacement keys (s. 24). Belongings: 'No landlord shall, without legal process, seize a tenant's property for default in the payment of rent' (s. 40), and the landlord's right to dispose of property left behind arises only after the unit has been vacated under a notice, an agreement, or a Board order (s. 41 (1)), none of which exists. Tyrone may apply to the Board for orders that the landlord altered the locking system without giving replacement keys and substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment or harassed him (s. 29 (1), paras. 3 to 5), within one year (s. 29 (2)). Because the unit is vacant, the Board may also order that the landlord allow him to recover possession and not rent the unit to anyone else (s. 31 (3)); that order has the effect of a writ of possession (s. 31 (4)) and expires after 15 days if not filed with the sheriff (s. 31 (5)). Other available orders include costs of replacing damaged or disposed-of property, out-of-pocket expenses, an abatement of rent and an administrative fine (s. 31 (1)). The arrears are a separate matter: the landlord's route is a non-payment notice (s. 59) and an application to the Board, not self-help.

story: For about 14 months the heating in Amira's Hamilton apartment broke down again and again. She bought space heaters, spent four nights in a hotel during a cold snap, and her rent was never reduced. She has added up a claim of $22,000 against her landlord and wants to file it in Small Claims Court because a coworker told her it is faster. She still lives in the unit.
question: Can Amira choose to sue her landlord in Small Claims Court for these losses instead of applying to the Landlord and Tenant Board? What happens to any amount she claims above the Board's monetary limit?
modelAnswer: A claim that the landlord failed to keep the unit in a good state of repair is a matter for the Board: a tenant may apply for an order determining that the landlord breached s. 20 (1) (s. 29 (1), para. 1), and the Board 'has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all applications under this Act' (s. 168 (2)). So she cannot simply choose a court for a claim the Board can hear. The Board may order payment of up to 'the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court' (s. 207 (1)); the Ministry of the Attorney General states that the Small Claims Court limit increased to $50,000 effective October 1, 2025, so the Board's limit is $50,000 and her $22,000 claim is within it. Only a person 'whose claim exceeds the Board's monetary jurisdiction' may start a proceeding in a court of competent jurisdiction, and that court can then exercise the Board's powers (s. 207 (2)). If she applies to the Board for an amount at or below its limit, 'all rights of the party in excess of the Board's monetary jurisdiction are extinguished once the Board issues its order' (s. 207 (3)), so she cannot later sue for the rest. Timing also matters: no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct occurred (s. 29 (2)), so the dates of each heating failure should be recorded.

story: Since early September 2026 nobody has seen Darnell, who rents a basement apartment in Peterborough from Ruth. Rent for September and October is unpaid and mail is piling up. Through the window Ruth can see a couch, a television, and a fridge full of spoiled food. Darnell has not given any notice. Ruth wants to clear everything out this weekend and re-rent the apartment on November 1. Ruth's insurance renewal is also due.
question: What must Ruth do before she can get rid of Darnell's belongings, and what rights does Darnell keep in them?
modelAnswer: A landlord shall not recover possession unless the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit or a Board order authorizes it (s. 39). If Ruth believes the unit is abandoned, she 'may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy' (s. 79). She may dispose of the property in an abandoned unit only if she obtains that order, or gives notice to the tenant and to the Board of her intention to dispose of the property (s. 42 (1)). Once the unit is abandoned, unsafe or unhygienic items, such as the spoiled food, may be disposed of immediately (s. 42 (2)). Everything else may be sold, kept or disposed of only after 30 days have passed from the order or the notice (s. 42 (3)). If, within those 30 days, Darnell notifies her that he intends to remove his property, he may remove it within that period, and she must make it available at a reasonable time and place close to the unit (s. 42 (4), (5)); she may first require payment of rent arrears and reasonable out-of-pocket costs of moving, storing or securing the property (s. 42 (6)). If within six months he claims property that she has sold, she must pay him the amount by which the sale proceeds exceed her reasonable expenses and any arrears (s. 42 (7)). A weekend clear-out without the order or notice is not what s. 42 permits.

story: Rosa runs a bakery in a strip plaza in Guelph under a five-year written lease. Rent of $4,000 is due on the first of each month. She did not pay the rent due June 1. The lease says nothing about re-entry or seizing goods. On June 17 the landlord's bailiff changed the locks. The landlord now also says it will seize and sell her two commercial ovens, which are inside, to cover the arrears. Rosa lives in a rented apartment across town. She has now raised the $4,000.
question: Does the Residential Tenancies Act or the Landlord and Tenant Board deal with this? What can a commercial landlord do when rent is unpaid, and how can Rosa try to get back into her premises?
modelAnswer: This is a commercial tenancy, governed by the Commercial Tenancies Act, not the residential regime; Ontario's guidance notes that if it is unclear whether a tenancy is residential or commercial, either party can ask the Landlord and Tenant Board to decide whether the Residential Tenancies Act applies. Re-entry: every lease is deemed to include an agreement that if rent 'remains unpaid for fifteen days after any of the days on which it ought to have been paid, although no formal demand thereof has been made', the landlord may re-enter (CTA, s. 18 (1)). Ontario's guidance gives the example that if rent was due January 1, the landlord may change the locks on January 17. Distress: alternatively, the landlord may seize and sell the tenant's goods on the premises, but the guidance states a landlord 'can change the locks and end the tenancy or seize and sell the tenant's property to cover unpaid rent. They can't do both.' Distress must be reasonable (s. 43), and goods seized may be sold only after five days following the distress and notice, and after appraisal by two sworn appraisers, with any surplus paid to the owner (s. 53). Relief: where a landlord is enforcing a right of re-entry or forfeiture, whether for non-payment of rent or other cause, the tenant may apply to the Superior Court of Justice for relief, which the court may grant on terms it considers just (s. 20 (1)). Where the landlord's proceeding is to enforce re-entry for non-payment and the tenant pays into court all the arrears and costs before judgment, 'the proceeding is forever stayed' (s. 20 (4)). If relief is granted, she holds the premises under the existing lease without a new lease (s. 20 (5)).

story: Owen owns a unit in a Toronto condominium, mortgaged to a bank. He is upset that the condominium corporation closed the pool for a year, and he has started a Small Claims Court action against the corporation over water damage to his unit. In protest he stopped paying his $650 monthly common expenses starting April 1, 2026. The property manager has told him the corporation will 'put a lien on the unit', but nothing has been registered yet. Owen also wants to repaint his balcony railing.
question: Can Owen withhold his common expenses for these reasons? What must the corporation do, and within what time, to keep a lien for the unpaid amount?
modelAnswer: Owners must contribute to the common expenses in the proportions in the declaration (s. 84 (1)), and an owner is not exempt even if the owner has waived or abandoned the right to use the common elements, is making a claim against the corporation, or is restricted from using them (s. 84 (3)). So neither the pool closure nor his lawsuit excuses non-payment. When an owner defaults, the corporation has a lien against the unit for the unpaid amount, interest, and reasonable legal costs and expenses of collection (s. 85 (1)). The lien 'expires three months after the default that gave rise to the lien occurred unless the corporation within that time registers a certificate of lien' (s. 85 (2)). At least 10 days before registering, the corporation must give Owen written notice of the lien (s. 85 (4)), and on or before registration it must give written notice to every encumbrancer registered on title, here the bank (s. 86 (3)). Once registered, the certificate covers the amounts under all unexpired liens and later defaults (s. 85 (3)). The lien has priority over registered and unregistered encumbrances, even earlier ones, subject to listed exceptions such as certain Crown and municipal tax claims (s. 86 (1)), and may be enforced in the same manner as a mortgage (s. 85 (6)). The railing is irrelevant.

story: Jun's car broke down on Highway 401 near Kingston. A tow truck took it to a vehicle storage yard. When Jun went to get his laptop from the back seat, the yard operator refused to let him take it until he paid the storage bill, and had not given him any invoice. Two days later Jun had the car taken to Pierre's garage. Pierre quoted $900 out loud to replace the alternator; there is no written agreement. Pierre now says the bill is $1,600 and will not release the car until it is paid in full. Jun's car is also overdue for an oil change.
question: What rights do the storage operator and Pierre have, and what can Jun do to get his laptop and his car back?
modelAnswer: Storage yard: under the Towing and Storage Safety and Enforcement Act, 2021, no vehicle storage operator 'shall retain anything found in a motor vehicle as a means of pressuring a person to make a payment' for towing or storage services (s. 24 (5)), so holding the laptop to force payment is prohibited. The operator must also let the owner have reasonable access to the vehicle during regular business hours (s. 24 (2)), and may not charge or demand payment for storage without first providing an invoice in accordance with the regulations (s. 27 (2)). Garage: under the Repair and Storage Liens Act, in the absence of a written agreement to the contrary, a repairer has a lien on the article it repaired and may keep it until paid, for the amount the customer agreed to pay or, where no amount was agreed, the fair value of the repair (s. 3 (1)). But no repairer's lien arises if the repairer was required to comply with sections 56 and 57, subsection 58 (1) and section 59 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2002 and has not done so (RSLA s. 3 (2)). Under the CPA, no repairer shall charge a consumer for any work or repairs unless the repairer first gives an estimate that meets the prescribed requirements (CPA s. 56 (1)), and for a vehicle that estimate must be in writing (O. Reg. 17/05, s. 48). A repairer may charge without an estimate only if it offered one, the consumer declined, the consumer specifically authorized a maximum amount, and the charge does not exceed it (CPA s. 56 (2)). Pierre's $900 was said out loud, so it is not a written estimate; whether he can charge anything, and so whether he has a lien at all, turns on whether the s. 56 (2) conditions were met. If they were, the lien cannot exceed the maximum amount Jun authorized (RSLA s. 3 (2.1) (b)), and the $1,600 bill is above $900. If Pierre does not get paid, he may sell the car under Part III after 60 days from when payment came due or the repair was completed (s. 3 (3)). To get the car back while disputing the amount, Jun may apply to the court where there is a dispute about the amount of the lien or the work authorized (s. 24 (1), (1.2)). He must pay into court, or post security for, the full amount claimed, or pay in an amount he offers in settlement and secure the balance (s. 24 (4)); on receiving the initial certificate, Pierre must release the car within three days unless he files a notice of objection (s. 24 (6)). The oil change is irrelevant.

invoice required before charging for storage (TSSEA s. 27 (2))
